analysis.one_liner: Diverts part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts with a government-guaranteed minimum retirement benefit.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2005 with two Republican cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers born in 1950 or later divert a slice of their Social Security payroll taxes — 5% of wages up to about $10,000, rising to 10%, plus 2.5% rising to 5% on wages above that — into personal savings accounts. Workers who opted in would give up traditional Social Security benefits earned on those wages, but the government would guarantee a monthly retirement income of at least 150% of the poverty line and top up any shortfall below the old benefit. Account money would be invested through a new federal board and, above a $25,000 balance, through investment options run by private investment companies. The bill also imposed new caps on the growth of entitlement and discretionary spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Investment companies, asset managers, recordkeepers, and custodians would gain a new stream of mandatory contributions to manage for fees. Younger workers who opted in would own accounts that pass to their heirs, get tax-free qualified distributions, and hold a federal guarantee that their retirement income never falls below 150% of poverty or below the old-style benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investment firms and participating younger workers

how_it_helps.text: Workers born on or after January 1, 1950 would be automatically enrolled (with a right to opt out) and would own personal accounts credited with their redirected payroll contributions, including earnings and losses.

The government would guarantee each participant at least a monthly payment equal to 150% of the poverty line, and would pay a top-up from the Social Security trust fund if the account-based annuity fell short of the traditional benefit the worker would have earned.
Amounts in the Savings Fund and approved investment options would be tax-exempt, and qualified distributions would be excluded from gross income.
The bill would provide for eventual reductions in FICA payroll tax rates as the program phases in.

analysis.who_pays: The transition would be financed by borrowing through a new transition fund while payroll revenue was diverted, adding to federal debt; the bill's own corporate-tax 'recapture' and spending-reduction formulas were estimates meant to refill the trust fund over decades. Participants would bear market risk on their accounts, traditional Social Security would lose a growing share of its revenue, and the bill's caps on entitlement and discretionary spending would put other programs under pressure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and future retirees bearing market risk

drawbacks.text: Diverting payroll contributions would drain revenue from the existing Social Security system for decades, requiring large-scale borrowing through a new 'Self-Liquidating Social Security Transition Fund' while benefits to current retirees still had to be paid.

Participants would lose entitlement to old-age benefits based on their own wages under section 202(z), so their retirement security would depend on investment returns — cushioned, but not eliminated, by the guarantee and top-up provisions.
Account balances invested in board-run funds and approved private investment options would be reduced by administrative expenses paid out of earnings, an annual cost disclosed to each participant.

The bill's new spending caps on entitlements and mandatories, enforced by a point of order against legislation, would constrain programs ordinary people rely on in order to make the transition arithmetic work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Participants would gain real ownership, heir-friendly accounts, and a genuine federal floor under their retirement income, but the guarantee would come at the price of a large, debt-financed transition and a slower erosion of the traditional system's finances. The guarantee formulas themselves rest on assumed long-term investment returns, so the promise would depend on markets and future Congresses honoring the top-up. As designed, the biggest, most certain winners were the financial firms that would manage the diverted money.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2005, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. John Sununu introduced the bill on April 20, 2005, joined by Sens. Sam Brownback and Jim DeMint; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill was one of the detailed personal-accounts proposals offered during the 2005 debate over Social Security, which produced no legislation in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security was left unchanged, so future beneficiaries kept the current benefit structure and taxpayers avoided a debt-financed transition. The investment industry gained nothing, since no mandatory accounts were created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of traditional Social Security; taxpayers

for.name: Sen. John E. Sununu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set out the full personal-accounts design, including the guarantee, transition fund, and spending caps.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Made private Social Security accounts the centerpiece of his 2005 domestic agenda and campaigned across the country for Congress to pass them, creating the political moment for bills like this one.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Finance Committee from April 2005 until the Congress ended with no further action.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Opposed any diversion of Social Security payroll taxes into private accounts during the 2005 debate and offered no support for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll-call to measure the split; all three sponsors were Republicans and the wider 2005 fight over personal accounts divided sharply by party, with Democrats uniformly opposed.

industries.note: The bill would have required every participating worker's payroll contribution to flow into accounts managed by professional asset managers, recordkeepers, and custodians under Board contract, and would have let investment companies offer approved Tier III options to workers with balances over $25,000 — a large new fee-paying customer base created by law. Workers would own the assets, but fees paid out of earnings and market risk would fall on them.

Tier I and fixed-income accounts could be invested in insurance contracts, giving insurers potential business, but retirement annuities would be issued by a new government Annuity Issuance Authority rather than by private insurers, cutting them out of the annuity market the accounts would create.
